steps.prompt: You are driving on an interstate highway in Tennessee. No speed limit sign is posted on this stretch. It is a clear day, and the road is dry. What is the fastest Tennessee law lets you drive here?
options: The fastest is 70 mph.
The fastest is 65 mph.
The fastest is 75 mph.

then.say: The fastest is 70 mph. That is the most Tennessee law allows on an interstate, and you drive that fast only when the conditions are ideal. Some stretches of interstate have a lower posted limit.

A stretch of interstate can have a lower posted limit, but no sign posts one here. The fastest Tennessee law lets you drive here is 70 mph, and you drive that fast only when the conditions are ideal.
75 mph is faster than Tennessee law allows on any interstate. The fastest is 70 mph, and you drive that fast only when the conditions are ideal.

steps.rule: The maximum speed set by Tennessee law for interstate highways is 70 mph, to be driven only in ideal conditions, and some stretches have a lower posted limit.

steps.prompt: You are driving on a state highway with one lane each way. No speed limit sign is posted on this stretch. It is a clear day, and the road is dry. What is the fastest Tennessee law lets you drive here?
options: The fastest is 55 mph.
The fastest is 45 mph.
The fastest is 70 mph.

then.say: The fastest is 55 mph. Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on primary and secondary state and federal highways is 55 mph. The 70 mph limit is set for interstates, and this road is not one.

45 mph would be the limit here only if a sign posted it, and no sign does. Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on a state highway is 55 mph.
70 mph is the limit set for interstates, and this road is not one. Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on a state highway is 55 mph.

steps.rule: Unless another speed is posted, the speed limit on primary and secondary state and federal highways is 55 mph.

steps.prompt: You are driving at night on a state highway with one lane each way. A sign says the speed limit is 55 mph. It is raining, and you cannot see far ahead. How fast do you drive?
options: You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark.
You drive at 55 mph, because that is the posted limit.
You drive faster than 55 mph, to get out of the rain sooner.
steps.answer: You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark.

then.say: You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark. The Basic Speed Rule says you drive at a speed that is safe for the conditions. The posted limit is only the most the law allows, not a speed that is always safe.

wrong.You drive at 55 mph, because that is the: The posted limit is only the most the law allows, not a speed that is always safe. In the rain and the dark you cannot see far ahead, so you drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe for the conditions.
wrong.You drive faster than 55 mph, to get out: Faster than 55 mph is over the posted limit, and the rain and the dark already make 55 mph too fast to be safe. You drive slower than 55 mph, at a speed that is safe in the rain and the dark.

steps.rule: The Basic Speed Rule teaches that you drive at a speed that is safe for the conditions, even when that is slower than the posted limit.

steps.prompt: On the interstate with no sign, on the state highway with no sign, and on the state highway in rain at night, what set the fastest you should drive?
options: The speed limit set the most, and the conditions could only lower the speed you may drive, never raise it.
The speed of the cars around you set it.
How fast your car can go set it.
steps.answer: The speed limit set the most, and the conditions could only lower the speed you may drive, never raise it.

then.say: The speed limit is the most you may drive on any road, even on a dry, clear day. A law or a sign cannot know when it is raining or dark, so you judge the conditions yourself and drive slower.

The cars around you did not set it. With no sign, the law set the most, 70 mph on the interstate and 55 mph on the state highway. In the rain at night, the conditions lowered the speed you should drive below 55 mph.
How fast your car can go did not set it. With no sign, the law set the most, 70 mph on the interstate and 55 mph on the state highway. In the rain at night, the conditions lowered the speed you should drive below 55 mph.

steps.prompt: You are following a car on a state highway. The car ahead passed a sign post at the side of the road. You said “one-thousand and one, one-thousand and two” to yourself, and then your car passed the same sign post. How far behind the car ahead are you?
options: You are two seconds behind it.
You are two car lengths behind it.
You cannot tell from this.
steps.answer: You are two seconds behind it.

then.say: You are two seconds behind it. Both cars passed the same sign post, and two seconds went by between them, so the gap between you is two seconds. This is how drivers measure their following distance, by counting the seconds between the car ahead passing a fixed point and their own car reaching it.

You counted the seconds between the car ahead passing the sign post and your car passing it, and a count of seconds tells you time, not car lengths. You are two seconds behind it.
Both cars passed the same sign post, and you counted the seconds between them, so the count tells you the gap. You are two seconds behind it.

steps.rule: To check your following distance, you count the seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed point, such as a sign post, until you reach the same point.

steps.prompt: You are following a car on a state highway on a dry day. The car ahead passed a sign post at the side of the road, and you started counting. Your car reached the sign post before you finished saying “one-thousand and two.” What do you do?
options: You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind.
You keep the same distance, because one second is enough.
You speed up to stay close to the car ahead.
steps.answer: You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind.

then.say: You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind. You reached the sign post in less than two seconds, so you were following too closely. After you slow down, you count again at another sign post or pole, until you finish “one-thousand and two” before you reach it.

wrong.You keep the same distance, because one: One second is too close: on a dry day you follow no closer than two seconds behind the car ahead. You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind, then count again at another sign post.
wrong.You speed up to stay close to the car ah: Speeding up brings you closer, and you already reached the sign post in less than two seconds. You slow down until you are at least two seconds behind.

steps.rule: Under normal conditions you follow no closer than two seconds, and when you reach the fixed point sooner, you slow down and check again until you are two seconds behind.

steps.prompt: You are driving on a state highway where the speed limit is 55 mph. It is a dry, clear day. You follow two seconds behind the car ahead. At what speeds on this road is two seconds enough?
options: Two seconds is enough at any speed on this road.
Two seconds is enough only up to 30 mph.
Two seconds is enough only up to 45 mph.
steps.answer: Two seconds is enough at any speed on this road.

then.say: Two seconds is enough at any speed on this road. The two-second rule holds at every speed on state and federal highways with moderate speed limits, like this one.

Two seconds is enough above 30 mph as well, and on this road you may drive up to 55 mph. On a state highway with a moderate speed limit, like this one, two seconds is enough at any speed.
Two seconds is enough above 45 mph as well, and on this road you may drive up to 55 mph. On a state highway with a moderate speed limit, like this one, two seconds is enough at any speed.

steps.rule: The two-second rule holds at any speed on state and U.S. highways with moderate speed limits.

steps.prompt: You are following a car on a state highway, and it is raining hard. What following distance do you keep?
options: You stay at least four seconds behind it.
You stay two seconds behind it, the same as on a dry day.
You stay one second behind it.
steps.answer: You stay at least four seconds behind it.

then.say: You stay at least four seconds behind it. Two seconds is not enough in bad weather, at night, or at higher speeds on the interstate. The extra distance lets you see more of the road ahead.

wrong.You stay two seconds behind it, the same: Two seconds is for normal conditions, and hard rain is bad weather. You stay at least four seconds behind the car ahead, which gives you more time to react.
One second is too close even on a dry day, when two seconds is the closest you follow. In hard rain you stay at least four seconds behind the car ahead.

steps.rule: In bad weather, at night, at higher interstate speeds, and behind a motorcycle, you follow at least four seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

steps.prompt: You are driving behind a motorcycle on a dry road in daylight. What following distance do you keep?
options: You stay at least four seconds behind it.
You stay two seconds behind it, the same as behind a car.
You stay one second behind it.
steps.answer: You stay at least four seconds behind it.

then.say: You stay at least four seconds behind it. Behind a motorcycle, two seconds is not enough, even on a dry road in daylight. The extra space gives you room to brake if the motorcycle stops suddenly.

wrong.You stay two seconds behind it, the same: Two seconds is for following a car in normal conditions, and behind a motorcycle you need more, even on a dry road in daylight. You stay at least four seconds behind it, which gives you room to brake if the motorcycle stops suddenly.
One second is too close even behind a car on a dry day, when two seconds is the closest you follow. Behind a motorcycle you stay at least four seconds back, which gives you room to brake if it stops suddenly.

steps.rule: In bad weather, at night, at higher interstate speeds, and behind a motorcycle, you follow at least four seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

steps.prompt: You are following a different car on a state highway and want to check how far behind it you are. The car ahead is about to pass a sign post at the side of the road. What do you do?
options: You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it.
You count the cars between you and the sign post.
You guess how many car lengths are between you and the car ahead.
steps.answer: You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it.

then.say: You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it. The sign post stays in one place, so the seconds between the two cars passing it are your following distance. If you reach it before you finish “one-thousand and two”, you are too close.

wrong.You count the cars between you and the s: Counting cars does not tell you how far behind the car ahead you are. You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it.
wrong.You guess how many car lengths are betwe: A guess does not measure anything. You count the seconds from when the car ahead passes the sign post until your car reaches it, because the sign post stays in one place.

steps.rule: To check your following distance, you count the seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed point, such as a sign post, until you reach the same point.

steps.prompt: Rear-end crashes, where a car hits the back of the car ahead of it, are very common. Most of them are caused by drivers doing one thing. What is it?
options: The drivers follow too closely, which is called tailgating.
The drivers use their turn signals.
The drivers drive with their headlights on.
steps.answer: The drivers follow too closely, which is called tailgating.

then.say: Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating. A driver who follows too closely cannot see the road past the car ahead, and has too little time to stop when it stops.

A turn signal tells the drivers around you what you plan to do, so using it does not cause a crash. Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating.
wrong.The drivers drive with their headlights: Headlights make your car easier for other drivers to see, so driving with them on does not cause a crash. Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating.

steps.rule: Most rear-end crashes are caused by drivers who follow too closely, which is called tailgating.

steps.prompt: You are driving past a school. A sign shows the speed limit for the school zone, which is lower than the limit on the rest of the road. When is that school zone speed limit in effect?
options: It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess.
It is in effect only from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. on weekdays, all year.
It is in effect all day and all night, every day of the year.
steps.answer: It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess.

then.say: It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess. Those are the times children are near the road, so the lower limit applies then, not at set hours of the clock and not all the time.

Two hours in the morning leave out the time children go home from the school and the school recess. The school zone limit is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess.
wrong.It is in effect all day and all night, e: The lower limit is not in effect all the time. It is in effect when children are going to or from the school, or during a school recess, because that is when children are near the road.

steps.rule: School zone speed limits are in effect when children are going to or from the school or during a school recess.

steps.prompt: Your car has anti-lock brakes, called ABS. The car ahead stops suddenly, and you must stop fast. How do you press the brake pedal?
options: You press it down firmly and hold it, without pumping.
You pump it quickly several times.
You press it, let it up, then press it again.
steps.answer: You press it down firmly and hold it, without pumping.

then.say: You press it down firmly and hold it, without pumping. Pumping the pedal or letting it up switches the anti-lock system off, so you keep steady pressure until the car stops. You may feel the pedal push back, which means the ABS is working.

Pumping the pedal switches the anti-lock system off. You press the pedal down firmly and hold it, with steady pressure, until the car stops.
wrong.You press it, let it up, then press it a: Letting the pedal up switches the anti-lock system off, the same as pumping it. You press the pedal down firmly and hold it, with steady pressure, until the car stops.

steps.rule: With anti-lock brakes, you press the brake pedal with firm, steady pressure and never pump it.

steps.prompt: You drove slower than 55 mph in the rain at night. You stayed four seconds behind a car in hard rain, and four seconds behind the motorcycle. What did driving slower and staying farther back give you?
options: They gave you more time to see a danger and react to it.
They gave you a shorter trip.
They gave you a better view of the cars behind you.
steps.answer: They gave you more time to see a danger and react to it.

then.say: The slower you drive and the farther back you stay, the more seconds you have before you reach a danger ahead, even though the trip takes longer. In those seconds you see the danger and brake or steer around it.

Driving slower and staying farther back make the trip longer, not shorter. They gave you more seconds to see a danger ahead and brake or steer around it.
wrong.They gave you a better view of the cars: Driving slower and staying farther back are about the road ahead of you, not the cars behind you. They gave you more seconds to see a danger ahead and brake or steer around it.
